Last month a band sent me a session for their single. It had a hundred and four tracks. I opened it and my first thought was: where is the singer? There were fourteen layers of backing vocals, a lot of synths, and so much reverb that the whole chorus sounded far away. The band had plenty of ideas, and that was the problem. So I muted everything except the drums, the bass and the lead vocal, and I added the other parts back one by one. If a part made the song better, it stayed. If it made hardly any difference, it went. In the end we kept about twenty tracks. The band was nervous at first. Nobody likes to hear that a few of their favorite ideas are not needed. But when they heard the new chorus, the singer said it was the first time she could hear her own voice. Very few changes in my job make people that happy.

I am the music director of a live singing show, and every week I have the same question: how much is too much? We have fifteen cameras, a band of nine, and a lot of lights, and the producers always want a little more. More dancers, more fire, more key changes. But a live show has only a few minutes for each song, and a singer has only a little air in her lungs. Last season, a young singer was given a huge arrangement with a choir and an orchestra on tape. In rehearsal, nobody could hear her. So we took away almost everything. We kept the piano, a few strings and her voice, and that was enough. She went to the final. I learned something that night. The audience does not count how many things are on the stage. They only remember one voice, and how much it made them feel.

The band sent a session with too many tracks. The engineer muted almost everything. He kept only a few parts: drums, bass and the lead vocal. He added the other parts back, one by one. Parts that made hardly any difference were deleted. The final chorus had enough energy and much less clutter.
